cf.title: Fix leak when a plpgsql exception block catches an error from CALL

input.subject: [PATCH] Fix leak when a plpgsql exception block catches an error from CALL

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at level 1a or 1b: message #1 gives a reproducible leak, its cause and measurements. The only surviving objection, maintenance-fit-1, is a small fixable design point at level 2. The fix changes which resource owner holds a plan pin and is meant for back-patch to 14 through 19, so a committer who knows the PL/pgSQL and SPI code has to sign for it. Nobody has replied yet.

brief.title: Fix plan pin leak when plpgsql exception block catches CALL error
brief.problem: A PL/pgSQL procedure that catches failing CALLs in an exception block keeps each failed CALL's plan until it returns, about 2 kB per failure. Batch procedures that log failed rows and go on can use memory without limit, about 2 GiB per million failures. DO blocks leak the same way, also in atomic contexts.
brief.proposed_design: exec_stmt_call() passes the procedure-lifespan resource owner to SPI only when SPI_inside_nonatomic_context() is true, that is, when the called procedure could end the transaction. Otherwise it leaves the owner NULL, so SPI uses the current resource owner, and aborting the exception block's subtransaction releases the pin. The patch also adds a regression test that counts CachedPlan contexts.
author_claims: The leak exists on master and on 14 through 19, as an oversight in commit ee895a655.
20,000 caught failures leave 20,005 extra CachedPlan contexts without the patch and 5 with it, and memory stays flat with or without COMMIT.
The extra test per CALL costs nothing measurable: 3.07s against 3.01s for 1,000,000 empty CALLs, within noise.
A per-CALL child resource owner also fixes the leak but costs about 3-4% per CALL.
The patch cherry-picks cleanly to 14 through 19 and should be back-patched, as a6b1f5365d5 was.
brief.thread_state: Only the first message is visible. Nobody has replied yet.
unclear: The author asks whether a regression test based on pg_backend_memory_contexts is too fragile, and no one has answered.
The author did not run the TAP tests, and the material does not say whether they pass.
The material does not say whether any extension or other PL depends on the current resource owner choice for atomic DO blocks.
The custom-plan-per-CALL cost the author mentions is left for later, with no proposal.

objections.title: Correctness depends on two copies of the non-atomic rule agreeing
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch changes when _SPI_execute_plan() runs a CALL non-atomically but leaves SPI_inside_nonatomic_context() unchanged. A CALL then runs non-atomically while its plan is pinned in the transaction's resource owner, and a COMMIT in the callee releases the pin while the plan is still in use. Users would hit this as a crash or a refcount warning on an uncommon path, long after the change was committed.
objections.argument: Message #1 says SPI_inside_nonatomic_context() "also implements" the rule from c96de42c4b5, which reads as a second copy of the rule that _SPI_execute_plan() applies, not a shared helper. After this patch, pl_exec.c relies on both copies giving the same answer to decide which resource owner holds the pin. The proposal does not say what fails loudly, such as an assertion, if the two copies drift apart. This is a small point for a back-patched bug fix, but a committer would likely ask for it before signing for the change on six branches.
objections.author_must_show: Do exec_stmt_call() and _SPI_execute_plan() share one test for non-atomic execution, or can an assertion catch a CALL that runs non-atomically while its pin is in the current resource owner?

critic.reasoning: spi.c does hold the rule twice: in _SPI_execute_plan() and in SPI_inside_nonatomic_context(). Drift would likely show as a plancache reference leak warning in the existing transaction tests, but the proposal does not say so, so the request for a shared test or assertion stands as a small point.

precedents_retrieved.title: Avoid use of TopMemoryContext for resource owner cleanup in portals
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves the freeing of failed portals' subsidiary memory contexts in At(Sub)Abort_Portals to after ResourceOwnerRelease during transaction abort. Resource owner cleanup code could then use memory below the portal, such as the executor context, so LLVM JIT, WaitEventSet and OpenSSL would no longer need TopMemoryContext allocations.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas held that anything needed for resource owner cleanup should live in TopMemoryContext, or in a dedicated child context of it. Under that rule, resource owners and memory contexts can be released in any order. He said the patch would add a hidden ordering dependency and make crashes more likely if a resource owner is released after its memory context is deleted. The author agreed to document the existing rule in the resource owner README.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think it's a good rule that anything that's needed for resource owner cleanup must be allocated in TopMemoryContext, so that there's no hidden dependency between resource owners and memory contexts and you can release them in any order.

precedents_retrieved.title: ResourceOwner refactoring
precedents_retrieved.summary: Heikki Linnakangas proposed replacing the per-kind arrays in ResourceOwner with one generic store: a small linear-searched array for recent entries plus a hash table for older ones. Each entry carries a kind with Release and PrintLeakWarning callbacks, so extensions can track their own resources the same way built-in code does.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier closed the entry because the latest patch no longer applied and had been waiting on author for weeks. Benchmarks in the thread showed the worst case still 24% slower than unpatched, and Aleksander Alekseev asked whether ResourceOwnerReleaseAll() could loop forever on the same entry. Neither question got an answer in the visible messages.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The latest patch does not apply anymore, and has been waiting on
author for a couple of weeks now, so switched as RwF for now.

precedents_retrieved.summary: Refactor ResourceOwner so that all tracked resource kinds share one small linear-searched array plus an overflow hash table, in place of a separate array per kind. Each kind defines Release and PrintLeakWarning callbacks, so extensions can track their own resources the way built-in code does, and lookups such as catcache references get faster.

precedents_retrieved.title: Dynamic result sets from procedures
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets a procedure return multiple result sets to the client by declaring cursors with `DECLARE ... CURSOR WITH RETURN` in its body, following DB2 and the SQL standard. A companion psql patch prints every result set of a command, where psql now shows only the last one.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Daniel Verite found bugs in the psql part: `\gexec` drops the first result and fails with FETCH_COUNT, multiple result sets do not work with FETCH_COUNT, `\errverbose` loses the last error, and PGresults leak. The author did not answer for two weeks, so Michael Paquier returned the patch with feedback. Robert Haas also asked whether one command returning several results breaks applications, and the author replied that the wire protocol already supports it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Peter, are you planning to answer to those complains? For now I am switching the patch as returned with feedback as this thread has no activity for two weeks.

precedents_retrieved.title: Dynamic result sets from procedures
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets a procedure declared with DYNAMIC RESULT SETS return the contents of cursors declared WITH RETURN as extra result sets of the CALL, following the SQL standard. It also lets the extended query protocol carry multiple result sets: a new RowDescription after Execute marks the start of each new set.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last visible messages, from February 2023, show the extended query protocol part breaking libpq pipeline mode and Alvaro Herrera's work-in-progress libpq fix. The author then split out a simple-query-only first patch and posted a new version, with no recorded objection after that.

precedents_retrieved.title: Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
Reverted commit(s): Further reduce overhead for passing plpgsql variables to the executor.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This patch does three interrelated things:

* Create a new expression execution step type EEOP_PARAM_CALLBACK
and add the infrastructure needed for add-on modules to generate that.
As discussed, the best control mechanism for that seems to be to add
another hook function to ParamListInfo, which will be called by
ExecInitExpr if it's supplied and a PARAM_EXTERN Param is found.
For stand-alone expressions, we add a new entry point to allow the
ParamListInfo to be specified directly, since it can't be retrieved
from the parent plan node's EState.

* Redesign the API for the ParamListInfo paramFetch hook so that the
ParamExternData array can be entirely virtual.  This also lets us get rid
of ParamListInfo.paramMask, instead leaving it to the paramFetch hook to
decide which param IDs should be accessible or not.  plpgsql_param_fetch
was already doing the identical masking check, so having callers do it too
seemed redundant.  While I was at it, I added a "speculative" flag to
paramFetch that the planner can specify as TRUE to avoid unwanted failures.
This solves an ancient problem for plpgsql that it couldn't provide values
of non-DTYPE_VAR variables to the planner for fear of triggering premature
"record not assigned yet" or "field not found" errors during planning.

* Rework plpgsql to get rid of the need for "unshared" parameter lists,
by dint of turning the single ParamListInfo per estate into a nearly
read-only data structure that doesn't instantiate any per-variable data.
Instead, the paramFetch hook controls access to per-variable data and can
make the right decisions on the fly, replacing the cases that we used to
need multiple ParamListInfos for.  This might perhaps have been a
performance loss on its own, but by using a paramCompile hook we can
bypass plpgsql_param_fetch entirely during normal query execution.
(It's now only called when, eg, we copy the ParamListInfo into a cursor
portal.  copyParamList() or SerializeParamList() effectively instantiate
the virtual parameter array as a simple physical array without a
paramFetch hook, which is what we want in those cases.)  This allows
reverting most of commit 6c82d8d1f, though I kept the cosmetic
code-consolidation aspects of that (eg the assign_simple_var function).

Performance testing shows this to be at worst a break-even change,
and it can provide wins ranging up to 20% in test cases involving
accesses to fields of "record" variables.  The fact that values of
such variables can now be exposed to the planner might produce wins
in some situations, too, but I've not pursued that angle.

In passing, remove the "parent" pointer from the arguments to
ExecInitExprRec and related functions, instead storing that pointer in a
transient field in ExprState.  The ParamListInfo pointer for a stand-alone
expression is handled the same way; we'd otherwise have had to add
yet another recursively-passed-down argument in expression compilation.

precedents_retrieved.title: Leaking memory in text_overlay function
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds explicit pfree calls to text_overlay in varlena.c to free the two substrings from text_substring and one intermediate concatenation result. The author argued that built-in functions should free the memory they allocate.
precedents_retrieved.objection: SQL-called functions run in short-lived memory contexts that are reset at the end of each tuple cycle, so not freeing memory in them is intentional. Adding retail pfree calls everywhere would make the system slower than a MemoryContextReset, and the patch showed no query-lifespan leak. The author accepted this and closed the thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There are places where it's important to avoid leaking memory, certainly.
But I don't think this is one of them, unless you can demonstrate a
scenario with query-lifespan or worse leakage.

precedents_retrieved.title: When deleting the plpgsql function, release the CachedPlan of the function
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Matthias van de Meent, Tom Lane
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch frees the CachedPlan contexts of a PL/pgSQL function or procedure when DROP FUNCTION or DROP PROCEDURE runs, so they no longer stay in CacheMemoryContext until the session ends. The author showed with pg_get_backend_memory_contexts() that a dropped and recreated procedure leaves two sets of CachedPlan contexts.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch frees cached plans only in the backend that runs the DROP, because other sessions do not execute RemoveFunctionById and keep their plans. Tom Lane suggested that PL/pgSQL, or funccache.c so SQL functions also benefit, install a shared-cache-invalidation callback on pg_proc that marks function trees as deletable. The author agreed, linked a new thread, and withdrew this entry. Vladlen Popolitov also asked why the plans should be freed at all.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It doesn't, which is (one reason) why it's just a crude hack.

precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 682ce911f modified exec_save_simple_expr to accept a Param
in the tlist of a Gather node, rather than the normal case of a Var
referencing the Gather's input.  It turns out that this was a kluge
to work around the bug later fixed in 0f7ec8d9c, namely that setrefs.c
was failing to replace Params in upper plan nodes with Var references
to the same Params appearing in the child tlists.  With that fixed,
there seems no reason to continue to allow a Param here.  (Moreover,
even if we did expect a Param here, the semantically correct thing
to do would be to take the Param as the expression being sought.
Whatever it may represent, it is *not* a reference to the child.)
Hence, revert that part of 682ce911f.

That all happened a long time ago.  However, since the net effect
here is just to tighten an Assert condition, I'm content to change
it only in master.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P12] and [P14] free CachedPlan contexts on DROP FUNCTION, a different leak with a different fix, and their recorded reason (other backends keep their plans) does not apply to a per-backend resource owner choice in exec_stmt_call(). Message #1 cites ee895a655 as the cause and a6b1f5365d5 as a back-patched fix for an earlier CALL leak, but neither is a rejected attempt at this fix.

From the standards and compatibility angle there is nothing to object to. The patch adds no syntax, GUC, catalog object or psql change, and it changes no dump output. The only behaviour change is which resource owner holds a plan pin during a CALL or DO. A CALL that cannot end the transaction now uses the current resource owner, as ee895a655 describes for atomic contexts, so the back-patch does not change any result a user can observe. Two points could not be checked without the code: whether the new test that reads pg_backend_memory_contexts behaves the same on every back branch, and whether any extension depends on the old resource owner choice for atomic DO blocks.

The patch changes only which in-memory resource owner holds a plan pin during CALL and DO in pl_exec.c. It adds no on-disk, WAL, catalog, wire protocol or exported struct change, so pg_upgrade, standbys, subscribers and the back-branch ABI are not affected. [P12] and [P14] dealt with freeing plans on DROP across sessions, a different problem.

The patch has no privilege or exposure aspect. It only changes which resource owner holds a plan pin for CALL and DO inside PL/pgSQL, adds no new object, role, setting or view, and lets no one see or do more than before. The leak it fixes affects only the session that runs the loop, and the patch removes that growth.

Apart from the point above, the fix looks like a fit for core: it is a narrow bug fix in pl_exec.c, it adds no new mechanism or API, and the author measured the cost per CALL. The precedents [P12] and [P14] concern freeing plans on DROP and do not apply here.

This is a bug fix for a memory leak, and no existing feature, setting or extension avoids the leak. The only workaround, force_generic_plan, still leaves a pin and a resource owner entry behind for each failure (message #1). The fix reuses existing SPI behaviour and SPI_inside_nonatomic_context(), so it adds no second mechanism. Precedents P12 and P14 cover cached plans freed on DROP FUNCTION, a different leak.

This is a bug fix for unbounded memory growth, and from the demand angle it should stand without field reports. Message #1 shows a reproducible leak of about 2 kB per caught CALL failure in a common batch pattern, and the cost falls on no one else, with no new UI and no measured per-CALL slowdown. [P12] and [P14] dealt with freeing plans at DROP time, and their reason does not apply here.
